theses.claim: Last year’s Q2 grew 4.9% year over year; repeating that rate on the FY2025Q2 base ($45,277m) would imply about $47,496m, roughly $386m above the forecast.
FY2026 Q1 net sales rose 4.8% YoY with comps positive, suggesting momentum; if Q2 growth lands modestly above the forecast’s implied ~4.05% (by ~0.75ppt), that would add about $340m.
Management’s FY2026 total sales growth guidance centers around ~3.5% (2.5%–4.5%); applying the midpoint to the FY2025Q2 base yields ~$46,862m, about $249m below the forecast.

Comparable sales are still muted (+0.6% in FY2026 Q1) and guided only flat to +2% for FY2026; if Q2 tracks the low-to-mid comp range, total sales growth would likely undershoot the forecast’s ~4.05% by a few tenths (~$200m).
The FY2026 sales and comp guidance is full‑year and does not specify quarterly cadence; timing/mix can shift dollars between quarters without changing the annual target.

rebuttals.0: Projecting FY2026 Q2 to “repeat” last year’s +4.9% is an unsupported what‑if. Management’s FY2026 total sales growth guidance tops out at 4.5% [7,8,9], and Q1 has already printed +4.8% YoY [0]. To remain within the annual range, there’s no evidence Q2 must run as high as 4.9%; the cited fact [28] only states last year’s rate, not that it will recur.
rebuttals.1: The “momentum” premise isn’t backed by the evidence. While Q1 net sales grew 4.8% YoY [0], comps were only +0.6% [6], and FY2026 guidance frames total sales growth at 2.5%–4.5% [7,8,9]. Claiming Q2 will run ~0.75 ppt above the forecast’s implied ~4.05% lacks support in the cited data; it’s a hypothetical rather than an evidenced driver [28].
rebuttals.2: Applying a full‑year growth midpoint (≈3.5%) directly to a single quarter is not supported. Guidance is annual and does not prescribe quarterly cadence [7,8,9], and Q1 already outpaced the midpoint at +4.8% [0]. Thus, using the midpoint to argue Q2 should be ~$249m below the forecast is a misuse of the cited guidance [28].
rebuttals.3: The inference that low comps imply total sales will undershoot the forecast isn’t supported. In FY2026 Q1, comps were +0.6% while total net sales rose +4.8% YoY [0,6], demonstrating material non‑comp drivers. Management also guides total sales growth (2.5%–4.5%) above comp growth (flat to +2%) [7,8,9,10,11,12], so mapping comp range to total growth—and a ~$200m shortfall off the forecast [28]—is not justified.
rebuttals.4: This point is supported: the FY2026 sales and comp guidance provided is for the full year and does not specify quarterly cadence [7,8,9,10,11,12], so timing can shift sales between quarters without changing the annual target.

theses.claim: Q1 adjusted EPS fell 3.7% y/y, yet management still guides FY2026 adjusted EPS to be flat to +4% versus $14.69, implying later quarters (starting with Q2) must run stronger, raising odds Q2 beats 4.642.
Demand momentum improved into FY2026: Q1 comps turned +0.6% vs -0.3% a year ago and net sales grew 4.8% y/y, pointing to a firmer top line that can lift Q2 EPS slightly above the forecast.
Comparable sales have been stabilizing/improving (FY2025 Q2 +1.0%, Q3 +0.2%, Q4 +0.4%, FY2026 Q1 +0.6%), suggesting modest operating leverage that could produce a small beat.
Despite 4.8% y/y sales growth in FY2026 Q1, adjusted EPS declined 3.7%, signaling margin pressure; if this persists, Q2 EPS may undershoot the 4.642 forecast by roughly 10–20 cents.
Q2 GAAP EPS has declined each year since FY2022 (5.05 → 4.65 → 4.60 → 4.58), indicating a downtrend in Q2 profitability that raises the risk FY2026 Q2 lands below the forecast.
Management’s FY2026 adjusted EPS outlook is only flat to +4%; with Q1 already down y/y, room for Q2 outperformance versus last year looks limited, biasing risk modestly below 4.642.
Only Q1 has reported adjusted EPS; Q2 history is GAAP-only, so inferring Q2 adjusted EPS from GAAP trends adds mapping uncertainty to the comparison.
FY2026 guidance ranges are full-year, not quarterly; without quarter-specific guidance, the timing of any acceleration is uncertain.

rebuttals.0: Full‑year guidance (flat to +4% vs $14.69) does not imply the acceleration must start in Q2; it can be back‑half weighted. With only Q1 adjusted EPS known and no quarter‑specific targets, there’s no evidence in the cites that Q2 must run above a 4.642 forecast. Also, last year’s Q2 adjusted EPS isn’t provided, so a “beat” case is not supported by the data cited.
rebuttals.1: Q1’s small comps uptick (+0.6%) and 4.8% sales growth did not prevent a 3.7% y/y decline in adjusted EPS, so stronger top line did not translate to earnings in Q1. Extrapolating that to a Q2 beat is speculative, and the cites provide no Q2‑specific margin or mix support to justify clearing 4.642.
rebuttals.2: The cited comps trend is essentially flat (from +1.0% to +0.6%), and Q1 adjusted EPS still fell y/y. That does not demonstrate operating leverage. Without evidence of margin expansion or cost leverage, the claim of a likely small beat lacks support from the provided data.
rebuttals.3: One quarter’s margin pressure does not establish persistence into Q2, and the claimed 10–20 cent shortfall is not substantiated by the citations. Moreover, the forecast presumably already reflects Q1 results; projecting an additional shortfall from Q1’s pattern alone is not supported.
rebuttals.4: The downtrend cited is GAAP EPS, while the forecast is adjusted EPS. Mapping GAAP to adjusted is uncertain, and the step‑downs since FY2022 include post‑pandemic normalization. The evidence does not directly support that FY2026 Q2 adjusted EPS should fall below 4.642.
rebuttals.5: A flat to +4% full‑year outlook does not constrain Q2 upside; acceleration can occur unevenly across quarters. The argument also mixes FY2025 Q2 GAAP EPS with an adjusted EPS forecast, an apples‑to‑oranges comparison, so the claimed downside bias to 4.642 isn’t supported by the cited facts.
rebuttals.6: This point is supported: the record provides Q2 GAAP EPS history but not Q2 adjusted EPS, while Q1 adjusted EPS is given. Inferring adjusted from GAAP adds acknowledged mapping uncertainty.
rebuttals.7: This is supported by the citations: guidance is full‑year only, so the timing of any intra‑year acceleration is indeed uncertain without quarter‑specific targets.

Q1 FY2026 showed strong net sales growth of 4.8% alongside positive comps, suggesting demand momentum that could lift Q2 comps above the 1.218% forecast.
Recent quarterly comps remain sub‑1% and are improving only gradually (0.2% → 0.4% → 0.6%), which projects to something closer to ~0.8–1.0% in Q2—below 1.218%.
The company’s FY2026 comparable‑sales guidance centers around ~1% (midpoint), anchoring expectations below the 1.218% forecast for an individual quarter.
Last year’s Q2 comparable sales increased only 1.0%, making a repeat near ~1.0% plausible absent a clear acceleration, which would undercut the 1.218% forecast.
Guidance is for the full year (0%–2%) and does not specify quarterly phasing, so it does not by itself indicate where Q2 will land within the range.
Net sales growth and comparable sales can diverge (e.g., Q1 FY2026 net sales +4.8% vs. comps +0.6%), so using sales growth to infer comps carries uncertainty.

rebuttals.0: The cited item is full‑year guidance up to 2.0% [12]; it does not indicate Q2 specifically. With Q1 comps only 0.6% [6], arguing Q2 will be “meaningfully above” 1.218% is speculative and not supported by the guidance alone.
rebuttals.1: Q1 comps were just +0.6% [6], not strong, and net sales growth (+4.8%) can reflect factors other than comps [0]. Using that sales growth to infer Q2 comps >1.218% lacks support; the linkage is not evidenced.
rebuttals.2: Projecting a linear step‑up from 0.2%→0.4%→0.6% [26,21,6] to “~0.8–1.0%” is an unsupported extrapolation from three points. It doesn’t rule out a print around or above 1.218%, and last year’s Q2 was already 1.0% [27], so the cited data don’t decisively imply <1.218%.
rebuttals.3: A 1% full‑year midpoint [11] does not anchor any single quarter below 1.218%. With Q1 at 0.6% [6], other quarters could reasonably run above 1% and still be consistent with full‑year guidance.
